title: Splitting the Flow: Baseflow Separation
description: Run the Lyne–Hollick digital filter interactively on a SYNTHETIC hydrograph with a known baseflow — drag the α slider to rewrite the live Python cell, compare filtered vs raw hydrographs side by side, and see why the Baseflow Index is a filter output rather than a measured groundwater fraction.

citation.text: Ladson, A. R., Brown, R., Neal, B. & Nathan, R. (2013). A standard approach to baseflow separation using the Lyne and Hollick filter. Australasian Journal of Water Resources, 17(1).

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: Capstone: A Basin's Water Story
description: Synthesis capstone for the Intro to Hydrology course. Choose one of four CAMELS-US basins, compute hydrological signatures (Lyne–Hollick BFI, Richards–Baker flashiness, flow-duration curve) from five years of observed daily flow, run the TWI pipeline on a synthetic hillslope, then narrate the basin's water story through a 6-stage timeline. Every number comes from a cell or from CAMELS.

citation.text: Newman, A. J. et al. (2015). Development of a large-sample watershed-scale hydrometeorological data set for the contiguous USA. Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci., 19, 209–223. See also Addor, N. et al. (2017), Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci., 21, 5293–5313, doi:10.5194/hess-21-5293-2017.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: Congratulations: Course Complete
description: Collect your name, preview a branded certificate of completion, and print or save it as a permanent record of finishing the Introduction to Hydrology course.

citation.text: AI-Hydro Learning Hub — Introduction to Hydrology (2026).

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: The Shape of the Land: DEM to TWI
description: Compute the Topographic Wetness Index from a DEM step by step — click cells to trace D8 flow paths computed in code, run the full fill → D8 → accumulation → slope → TWI pipeline on a synthetic hillslope, explore a 3-D terrain, and compare elevation vs wetness with a wipe slider. Includes D8 vs D∞ and the effect of the slope floor and DEM resolution.

citation.text: Beven, K.J. & Kirkby, M.J. (1979). A physically based, variable contributing area model of basin hydrology. Hydrol. Sci. Bull., 24(1), 43–69.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: The Return Flow: Evapotranspiration and the Budyko Curve
description: Compute potential evapotranspiration two ways (Hargreaves–Samani and Priestley–Taylor) from real Daymet weather, reproduce the tabulated CAMELS pet_mean as a check, derive long-term actual evapotranspiration from P − Q, and place 670 CAMELS basins in Budyko space with a Fu curve whose ω you fit yourself.

citation.text: Zhang, L., Hickel, K., Dawes, W. R., Chiew, F. H. S., Western, A. W. & Briggs, P. R. (2004). A rational function approach for estimating mean annual evapotranspiration. Water Resources Research.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: Rain and Snow: From Gauge to Basin
description: From a rain gauge to a basin average: build the arithmetic, Thiessen and inverse-distance estimates on a synthetic storm field you can inspect completely, then use real CAMELS-US Daymet precipitation for four basins to see how hard, how often and when it falls, test a rain-snow temperature threshold, and reproduce two CAMELS climate attributes with a live Python cell.

citation.text: Newman, A. J. et al. (2015). Development of a large-sample watershed-scale hydrometeorological data set for the contiguous USA. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 19, 209-223.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: Reading a Hydrograph
description: Anatomy of a storm hydrograph — rising limb, peak, recession — with an interactive BFI explorer on a synthetic event, a curve-number storm-pair comparison showing non-linear runoff response, and a live Python cell that plots a real CAMELS-US water year (observed flow and basin precipitation) for three contrasting gauges.

citation.text: Ladson, A. R., Brown, R., Neal, B. & Nathan, R. (2013). A standard approach to baseflow separation using the Lyne and Hollick filter. Australasian Journal of Water Resources, 17(1).

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: Catching the Flow: Real Streamflow Data
description: Load five real water years of USGS daily streamflow for four curated CONUS gauges from a bundled CAMELS-US snapshot (offline, with source hashes and QC flags). Plot the annual regime, spot flood days and rank annual maxima with Weibull plotting positions. An optional live NWIS cell reports failures instead of substituting data.

citation.text: Newman, A. J. et al. (2015). Development of a large-sample watershed-scale hydrometeorological data set for the contiguous USA. Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci., 19, 209–223. See also Addor, N. et al. (2017), Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci., 21, 5293–5313, doi:10.5194/hess-21-5293-2017.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: Runoff Generation: Infiltration Excess and Saturation Excess
description: Two ways rain becomes runoff. Compute Green–Ampt ponding and infiltration on a SYNTHETIC soil column with a finite storage deficit, map which mechanism wins over rain intensity and deficit, watch the saturated area of a SYNTHETIC hillslope grow with storm depth, then compute event runoff coefficients from real CAMELS-US daily rain and flow for three basins and see why daily data cannot identify the mechanism.

citation.text: Dunne, T. & Black, R.D. (1970). Partial area contributions to storm runoff in a small New England watershed. Water Resources Research, 6(5), 1296–1311.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: The Water Cycle in Motion
description: Trace a water molecule through all six fluxes — evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff — via a Manim animation and a slider-driven cycle diagram. Compute the dew-point and dry-adiabatic lapse rates from physical constants, then use a mass-conserving bucket to see why P = ET + R + ΔS.

citation.text: Trenberth, K.E. et al. (2007). Estimates of the global water budget. J. Hydrometeorol., 8(4), 758–769.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University

title: The Watershed: Where Rain Becomes Runoff
description: Define a catchment, trace D8 flow paths across a SYNTHETIC 3-D terrain (depression-filled, drop/distance routing, stream network from flow accumulation), orbit a real basin (the Fish River, Maine, from the Copernicus GLO-30 DEM) and drop rain on it, then turn rainfall into runoff with an executable rational-method cell and an SCS curve-number cell.

citation.text: O'Callaghan, J.F. & Mark, D.M. (1984). The extraction of drainage networks from digital elevation data. Comput. Vision Graph. Image Process., 28(3), 323–344.

author: Mohammad Galib, Purdue University
